name: Buxa Tiger Reserve and Buxa Fort
tagline: A Bhutanese fort, a freedom fighters' jail and a forest that climbs to Bhutan
meta_description: Buxa Tiger Reserve and Buxa Fort guide: the trek from Santalabari, Lepchakha village, history as a detention camp, birding, permits, costs and stays.
summary: Buxa Tiger Reserve covers 760 sq km of forest in Alipurduar district, from 60 m in the plains to 1,750 m at the Bhutan border. Its highlight for visitors is Buxa Fort, a Bhutanese frontier post that became a British detention camp, reached by a one-hour walk from Santalabari, with Lepchakha village half an hour above. Tigers are very rarely seen.
intro: Buxa is the eastern end of the Bengal Dooars and the wildest part of it. The reserve stretches from flat forest near Rajabhatkhawa up through steep, wooded hills to the Bhutan border, where it joins Bhutan's Phibsoo sanctuary, with Manas to the east. Elephants move freely across this landscape. It was declared India's fifteenth tiger reserve in 1983, but tigers are now extremely rare here; come for the forest, the birds and the history, not for a big cat.

The story most visitors come for is Buxa Fort. It sits at about 867 m on the old Buxa Duar route into Bhutan, and you reach it by a walk of about 2.5–5 km, an hour or so, from the road end at Santalabari. The Bhutanese built it to guard the pass; the British took it, and in the 1930s turned it into a high-security detention camp for Indian revolutionaries. Later it sheltered Tibetan monks who fled in 1959. Today it is a set of ruined walls in the forest with a small memorial.

Half an hour above the fort, the Drukpa village of Lepchakha sits on a ridge with a small chorten and one of the best views in North Bengal: on a clear day, several rivers of the Dooars shining across the plains far below. Homestays here and at Santalabari make an overnight possible. Rajabhatkhawa, at the foot of the reserve, has the forest office, a nature interpretation centre and the start of jeep safaris.

story.title: From Bhutanese pass fort to political prison
paras: Buxa Fort guarded the Buxa Duar, one of the eighteen passes between the plains and Bhutan, on the route that connected Bhutan and Tibet with Bengal. In 1772, after the East India Company intervened in Cooch Behar, Company troops took the fort; Bhutan got it back under the peace of 1774. During the Duar War of 1864–65 a British column occupied it again, and the Treaty of Sinchula in November 1865 confirmed British control.

The British rebuilt the fort in brick, granite and lime, and from 1930 to 1937 used it as a detention camp under the Bengal Criminal Law Amendment Act, holding revolutionaries far from their supporters. It was used again as a special jail in the 1940s and early 1950s. Rabindranath Tagore wrote verses for the detainees. In 1959, monks of Drepung Monastery who had fled Tibet set up a study centre, Buxa Chogar, here; they moved to Karnataka in 1971.
story.source: Wikipedia 'Buxa Fort' and 'Duar War'; Treaty of Sinchula (1865)

did_you_know: Buxa Fort was used as a detention camp for Indian revolutionaries from 1930 to 1937, and later as a special jail.
From 1959 to 1971, monks of Drepung Monastery who had fled Tibet ran a monastic study centre called Buxa Chogar at the fort.
Buxa Tiger Reserve, created in 1983 as India's fifteenth tiger reserve, records at least 284 bird species.

highlights.title: The walk to Buxa Fort
highlights.text: From the road end at Santalabari, a stone path climbs through forest to the fort in about an hour. It is steady rather than steep, and porters and local guides are available. Start by 9 a.m. in the warmer months.

highlights.title: Lepchakha's view of the Dooars
highlights.text: Half an hour above the fort, the Drukpa village of Lepchakha has a small chorten on a ridge. On clear winter days you see the Dooars plains with several rivers, including the Jayanti, shining far below.

highlights.title: History you can stand in
highlights.text: The fort's ruined walls, cell blocks and memorial tell the story of the detention camp and the later Tibetan refugee centre. Read up before you go; signage is limited.

highlights.title: Birding across altitudes
highlights.text: With forest from 60 m to 1,750 m, Buxa holds at least 284 bird species. Hornbills, barbets, laughingthrushes and many migrants are possible on the walk and around Rajabhatkhawa.

highlights.title: Rajabhatkhawa gateway
highlights.text: The village at the foot of the reserve has the forest office, a nature interpretation centre and the start of jeep safaris into the plains section of the reserve.

how_to_reach.text: From Siliguri drive about 180 km via Malbazar, Birpara, Hasimara and Rajabhatkhawa to Santalabari, four and a half to five hours. From Madarihat it is about 2 hours, and from Alipurduar about 30 km, 1 hour. A reserved car from Siliguri costs ₹5,500–7,000, indicative 2026.

Alipurduar Junction is the nearest major station, with trains from Siliguri and Kolkata including the Kanchankanya Express. Rajabhatkhawa station is also on the line. From Alipurduar, take a car to Santalabari for about ₹1,200–2,000, indicative 2026.

From Santalabari, walk to Buxa Fort in about an hour on a stone and earth path, and on to Lepchakha in another half hour. A longer trail continues through the forest to Jayanti, about 13 km, with a guide.

where_to_stay: Santalabari, at the start of the walk, and Lepchakha above the fort have simple homestays with shared or basic attached bathrooms and home-cooked meals, roughly ₹1,500–2,500 per person including food, indicative 2026. Rajabhatkhawa and Jayanti have more lodges and forest-department accommodation. Alipurduar town, an hour away, has standard hotels. Book homestays through local contacts or a trusted agent.
costs: Forest entry for the Buxa Fort walk
Local guide to the fort and Lepchakha
budget_tip: Take the train to Alipurduar, a shared or hired car to Santalabari, and stay a night at a Lepchakha homestay with meals; it costs less than one night at a Dooars resort.
tips: Get your forest entry ticket at the checkpoint before Santalabari and carry ID.
Wear trekking shoes with grip; the path is stony and slippery after rain.
Start early: by 11 a.m. in April and May the climb is hot and humid.
Do not come for tigers; sightings are extremely rare, and the reserve's value is its forest, birds and history.
The reserve closes from 16 June to 15 September; check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: The walk up to Buxa Fort
experiences.summary: From Santalabari a stone path climbs through forest to the ruins of Buxa Fort at about 867 m. It takes about an hour up at an easy pace. At the top are broken walls, old cell blocks and a memorial to the political prisoners held here.
body: The walk starts at the road end at Santalabari, where you register, pay the forest fee and can hire a guide or porter. The path is wide, partly paved with stones, and climbs steadily through mixed forest of tall trees, bamboo and ferns. Butterflies are everywhere in October and November, and birds call from the canopy. Allow about an hour up and 45 minutes down.

At the top, the fort is less a fort than a set of ruins: sections of thick wall, gateways, building foundations and the remains of the camp where detainees were held in the 1930s and later. A memorial remembers them. Walk around slowly and imagine the place as it was, deep in Bhutan border forest, far from Calcutta.

Carry water, a snack and a rain jacket. The path is slippery after rain and can have leeches from April. Guides can tell stories of the camp and the Tibetan monks who lived here from 1959. Continue to Lepchakha if you have energy and time, or stay overnight in a homestay.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Buxa Fort trek
faqs.a: Easy to moderate. It is a steady climb of about an hour on a wide stone path from Santalabari, gaining a few hundred metres. Most reasonably fit people, including older children, manage it. Go slowly, carry water and wear shoes with grip. Porters are available.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Buxa Fort
faqs.a: You need a forest entry ticket, paid at the checkpoint on the way to Santalabari, and photo ID. A local guide is recommended. Rules and fees change, and the reserve closes from 16 June to 15 September. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Who was imprisoned at Buxa Fort
faqs.a: From 1930 to 1937 the British used the fort as a detention camp for Bengal revolutionaries held without trial under the Bengal Criminal Law Amendment Act. It was used again as a special jail in the 1940s and early 1950s. The poet Subhash Mukhopadhyay was among those held there in a later period.

experiences.title: Lepchakha and the view of the Dooars rivers
experiences.cost: ₹1,500–2,500 per person for homestay with meals, indicative
experiences.summary: Above Buxa Fort, the Drukpa village of Lepchakha sits on a ridge with a small chorten and a sweeping view over the Dooars. On a clear winter morning you see several rivers threading across the plains. Homestays make it possible to stay the night.
body: From the fort, a path climbs another half hour to Lepchakha, a small village of Drukpa families who have lived on this ridge for generations. Houses are of wood and stone, with prayer flags and vegetable gardens. At the edge of the village a small chorten stands above a steep drop, and from here the plains open out below.

On a clear morning between November and February, you can pick out several rivers of the Dooars, including the Jayanti, Bala and Dima, as bright lines across the forest and fields; on the very best days locals say more are visible. Sunrise and early morning give the clearest air before haze builds.

Lepchakha homestays offer simple rooms, shared bathrooms in many cases, and home-cooked meals of rice, dal, vegetables and sometimes local cheese or meat. Electricity and signal can be unreliable. Bring a torch and warm clothes, and respect the chorten: walk around it clockwise and do not climb on it.

faqs.q: Who lives in Lepchakha
faqs.a: Lepchakha is a Drukpa village, a community with cultural links to Bhutan that has lived on this ridge above Buxa Fort for generations. Many families now host visitors in homestays alongside farming. Be respectful of the chorten and of people's homes, and ask before taking photos.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight at Lepchakha
faqs.a: Yes. Several families run simple homestays, about ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals, indicative 2026. Rooms are basic and bathrooms often shared. Book through local contacts or a trusted agent; walk-ins may find space midweek but not on holiday weekends.

faqs.q: What can I see from Lepchakha
faqs.a: On clear days, the forests and plains of the Dooars stretching south, with several rivers, including the Jayanti, Bala and Dima, visible as bright channels. Haze often hides the far view after February. Winter mornings soon after sunrise are best.

experiences.title: Rajabhatkhawa nature centre and jeep safari
experiences.summary: Rajabhatkhawa, at the foot of the reserve, has the forest office, a nature interpretation centre and the start of jeep safaris through the plains forest of Buxa. Elephants, gaur and deer are the likely sightings.
body: Rajabhatkhawa is a small village on the road from Alipurduar to Jayanti, surrounded by forest. The nature interpretation centre here explains the reserve's habitats, from riverine grassland to hill forest, and its role as a corridor linking India and Bhutan. It makes a good first stop to understand what you will see.

Jeep safaris are run by the forest department through the plains sections of the reserve. Expect sal and mixed forest, river crossings, and sightings of elephants, gaur, sambar, barking deer, wild boar and many birds. Leopards and clouded leopards live here but are rarely seen; tigers are now extremely rare.

Book safaris at the Rajabhatkhawa or Jayanti counters or through the forest department's booking system, and check which routes are open. Morning slots are best. Combine with a night at Jayanti or Santalabari. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I see a tiger in Buxa Tiger Reserve
faqs.a: It is extremely unlikely. Although Buxa was declared a tiger reserve in 1983, tigers became very rare, and only occasional camera-trap records have been reported in recent years. Come for elephants, gaur, birds, forest and history. Do not book Buxa for a tiger sighting.

faqs.q: How do I book a Buxa jungle safari
faqs.a: Jeep safaris are organised by the forest department and booked at counters in Rajabhatkhawa or Jayanti, or through its booking system where available. Routes and timings vary by season. Ask your lodge to help, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is at the Rajabhatkhawa nature centre
faqs.a: The nature interpretation centre has displays on Buxa's forests, wildlife and the people who live around it, and explains the reserve's role as a corridor with Bhutan. It is a short, useful stop before a safari or trek. Hours vary; it is usually open in daytime.

experiences.title: Birding on the Buxa hill trails
experiences.cost: ₹800–2,000 for a local birding guide, indicative
experiences.summary: With forest from the plains to 1,750 m, Buxa has one of the richest bird lists in Bengal, at least 284 species. The paths around Santalabari, Buxa Fort and Lepchakha are good for hill and foothill birds.
body: The trail from Santalabari to Buxa Fort and Lepchakha passes through several forest types in a short climb. At dawn, listen for mixed flocks: minivets, flycatchers, warblers, fulvettas and yuhinas moving through the canopy. Laughingthrushes call from the undergrowth, and barbets from the tops of trees. Great and wreathed hornbills are possible, as are raptors circling over the ridge.

Lower down, around Rajabhatkhawa and Jayanti, river and forest-edge birds add to the list: kingfishers, river lapwings, redstarts in winter, bee-eaters and drongos. With a local guide who knows calls, a morning can easily produce 50 or more species.

Stay on the main trails with your guide; Buxa has elephants and the forest is dense. Carry binoculars, water and a light jacket. Combine birding with the fort walk and a night at Lepchakha to catch both dawn and dusk on the ridge.

faqs.q: How many bird species are there in Buxa
faqs.a: Buxa Tiger Reserve records at least 284 bird species, thanks to its range of habitats from 60 m in the plains to 1,750 m at the Bhutan border. Hornbills, barbets, laughingthrushes, minivets and many winter migrants are among them.

faqs.q: Where is the best birding in Buxa
faqs.a: The trail from Santalabari to Buxa Fort and Lepchakha is excellent for hill and foothill forest birds at dawn. Around Rajabhatkhawa and Jayanti, rivers and forest edges add waterbirds and edge species. A local birding guide makes a big difference.

faqs.q: When is the best season for birding in Buxa
faqs.a: November to April. Winter brings migrants and clear mornings; March and April bring breeding calls and more activity. The reserve closes from 16 June to 15 September. Early mornings are always best.

faqs.q: How do I reach Buxa Fort from Siliguri
faqs.a: Drive about 180 km via Malbazar, Birpara, Hasimara and Rajabhatkhawa to Santalabari, four and a half to five hours, then walk about an hour to the fort. Alternatively, take a train to Alipurduar and a car to Santalabari, about an hour. A reserved car from Siliguri costs ₹5,500–7,000, indicative 2026.

faqs.q: How long is the Buxa Fort trek
faqs.a: From Santalabari the walk to the fort takes about an hour up and 45 minutes down. Continuing to Lepchakha adds about 30 minutes each way. The whole outing, with time at the fort and village, takes three to five hours. A longer trail continues to Jayanti, about 13 km, with a guide.

faqs.q: Is Buxa Tiger Reserve worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, for forest, birds, history and walking, especially Buxa Fort and Lepchakha. It is not the place for easy big-mammal sightings, and tigers are extremely rare. If you want rhinos and gaur, pair Buxa with Jaldapara, about two hours away.

faqs.q: When is Buxa Tiger Reserve closed
faqs.a: Like other Dooars protected areas, Buxa closes to visitors from 16 June to 15 September for the monsoon and breeding season. Some areas may also close at short notice. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Where should I stay for Buxa Fort
faqs.a: For the fort and views, stay in a homestay at Santalabari or Lepchakha. For more comfort and safaris, stay at Jayanti or Rajabhatkhawa. Alipurduar town, an hour away, has standard hotels. Book homestays in advance through local contacts.

faqs.q: Is Buxa Fort suitable for children and seniors
faqs.a: Children of about seven and up who walk regularly usually manage the hour-long climb. Seniors who are fit and walk daily can do it slowly; porters carry bags. People with heart or knee problems should think carefully, as the path is steady uphill and uneven.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network at Buxa Fort and Lepchakha
faqs.a: Signal is patchy on the trail and at Lepchakha, sometimes available on one network on the ridge. Electricity can be unreliable. Download what you need, carry a power bank and torch, and tell family you may be offline.

faqs.q: What is the history of Buxa Fort
faqs.a: A Bhutanese fort guarding the Buxa Duar pass, it was captured by the East India Company in 1772, returned in 1774, retaken in the Duar War of 1864–65 and kept under the Treaty of Sinchula. The British used it as a detention camp from 1930 to 1937 and later as a jail. Tibetan monks used it from 1959 to 1971.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Buxa
faqs.a: Yes. Foreign visitors can visit Buxa Tiger Reserve and Buxa Fort with the normal forest entry ticket and their passport. The area is close to the Bhutan border, so carry ID and follow instructions at checkpoints. Check current status before you travel.
